newsitem.title: USA: Swallows return to Capistrano a few days early.
newsitem.headline: Swallows return to Capistrano a few days early.

text.p: Following an annual spring rite more than two centuries old, swallows returned to the San Juan Capistrano Mission on Saturday, greeted by the ringing of bells.
But the little birds also were greeted by the grumbling of traditionalists, who were upset that the old Spanish mission was celebrating four days early in an effort to lure more tourist dollars.
The swallows have returned every March 19 -- St. Joseph's Day -- in the 214-year history of the mission, their impeccable timing a cause for both celebration and wonder.
Last year, mission officials decided to start holding the annual celebration on a weekend in the hope that weekend festivities would bring in more visitors -- angering many in the area.
Caynel Wald, director of the mission's visitors' centre, on Saturday shrugged off what she said was a still-simmering controversy.

"The traditional day was the 19th, but is that the day the swallows always returned? No," she said. "They return whenever they feel like it. It has more to do with climate and food supply than anything else."
Wald said it took the birds almost two months to make the trip north to Capistrano from their winter quarters in Goya, Argentina, and the exact moment of arrival was unpredictable.
"They come in mid-March, truthfully, and we celebrate their return," she said. "After all, that's a mean feat for a bunch of little birds."
Wald, who was dressed for the day as a Spanish senora from the 1820's, said the swallows had been returning to Capistrano since even before the mission was founded in 1776.
"They used to nest in the cliffs down along the ocean," she said, but probably found the eaves of the mission buildings a little more comfortable.
"In fact, every spring we get calls from homeowners saying 'I have your darn swallows and I do not want them'," Wald added.

Plenty of the birds were in sight during Saturday's daylong celebration, including one building a nest not far from where vendors sold souvenirs and a stage where performers sang the 1939 hit "When the Swallows Come Back to Capistrano."
The birds' return has been celebrated since 1910, when Father St. John O'Sullivan was posted at the mission.

Father O'Sullivan became fascinated with the swallows' migratory cycle and viewed their return as inspiring renewal and a rejuvenation of the human spirit. He eventually wrote a book on the phenomenon, called "Capistrano Nights."
